subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 5 periods = 250 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 4h 10min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem and Exploring Central Ideas

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.245): oral warm-up — emotions at the base of a challenge
Check Your Understanding (p.247): identify central idea for each stanza
Check Your Understanding (p.247): true/false on tone — motivational and shifting

time_bands.activity: Warm-up using Reflect and Respond (p.245): students share orally what emotions they feel at the base of a difficult task and what might prompt a first step. Teacher accepts two or three quick responses to open the conversation.
Unhurried read-aloud of the poem — teacher models first, then students take turns reading stanza by stanza, attending to punctuation and tone. Textbook open to p.245–247.
Paired discussion using Check Your Understanding (p.247): pairs select the central idea for each of the four stanzas, then report back. Teacher builds a class consensus on the board.

Quick whole-class check using Check Your Understanding (p.247): students judge the two tone statements as true or false, justifying with a line from the poem. Teacher draws out the motivational shift from stanza one to stanza four.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem addresses the reader directly through 'you', so prompt students to feel the speaker as a guide rather than a stranger — this is the heart of the intimate tone described in the appreciation summary. Students commonly conflate the motivational tone with an optimistic one; the appreciation summary notes a thoughtful quality in the early stanzas, so draw out that shift. Task on personal challenges (task index 1) is unanchored here and may be set as a brief reflective note in students' own time.

periods.activity_title: Devices, Symbolism, and Critical Reflection on the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.248–249): explain the metaphor in 'The first step is the hardest'
Reading for Appreciation (p.248–249): identify lines showing antithesis and explain
Critical Reflection (p.250–251): four extended-answer questions on metaphor, antithesis, realism, and personal application

homework.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.248–249): symbolism fill-in — comfort/status quo, future, first step

time_bands.activity: Brief re-reading of stanzas three and four aloud, then close analysis of the metaphor task from Reading for Appreciation (p.248–249): students explain in writing why 'The first step is the hardest' is metaphorical. Teacher takes two or three responses and consolidates.

Close-reading of antithesis: students locate the lines from Reading for Appreciation (p.248–249) where opposing ideas are held in tension, then explain the effect in one sentence each. Class shares and teacher connects to the appreciation summary's note on antithesis as a central device.

Unhurried independent written response to the four Critical Reflection questions (p.250–251) covering the significance of the metaphor, the message of antithesis, evaluation of the poem's realism, and personal connection to self-belief. Teacher circulates and offers brief formative prompts.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud and identified central ideas per stanza, students are ready to examine the craft. The appreciation summary identifies antithesis as the dual pull of 'pull you forward / push you back' — draw attention to this exact phrasing so students do not search the whole poem aimlessly. The symbolism task (task index 9) is moved to homework because anchoring it fully alongside the four extended-answer questions would exceed the time available.

periods.activity_title: Latin Expressions and Rhetorical Questions in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary in Context (p.251–252): fill blanks with six Latin expressions from the table
Vocabulary in Context (p.252): state what two rhetorical questions intend to achieve
Vocabulary in Context (p.252–253): match six situations to appropriate rhetorical questions

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept that 'status quo' — used in the poem — is a Latin expression still active in English, and briefly presents the six Latin terms in the table (p.251). Students read the table silently and predict meanings from context.
Students complete the fill-in task from Vocabulary in Context (p.251–252) using the six Latin expressions in the given sentences. Pairs compare answers before whole-class verification.

Teacher presents the definition of rhetorical question and connects it to the poem's own line 'Will it pull you forward / or push you back in fear?' Students then write what each of the two given rhetorical questions intends to achieve (Vocabulary in Context, p.252).

Matching activity from Vocabulary in Context (p.252–253): students link six real-life situations to the most fitting rhetorical question. Pairs work together, then teacher conducts a quick class check, asking students to justify one or two of their choices.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's own rhetorical question provides a ready anchor — use it to show that rhetorical questions signal urgency, not inquiry, before moving to the exercise. Students sometimes confuse exempli gratia (e.g.) and et cetera (etc.) in usage; briefly distinguish them when reviewing the Latin table. The 'status quo' meaning task from Reading for Comprehension (task index 3, p.245) is closely related but was not anchored earlier; flag it as useful self-study alongside the Latin expressions work.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Self-Belief and Proverb Role-Plays

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.253): answer three questions in one-to-three exact words heard
Listen and Respond (p.253): select the four true statements from seven
Speaking Activity (p.254–255): paired role-plays using three proverbs in real-life situations

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets context: students will hear a conversation between two school friends, Karan and Ananya, just before a school play. Students open notebooks and prepare to write key words heard.

First listen — teacher reads the transcript aloud once at natural pace; students answer the three short-response questions from Listen and Respond (p.253) in one-to-three exact words. Second listen — teacher reads again; students select the four true statements from the seven given (p.253). Class verification follows.

Transition to speaking: teacher presents the three proverbs from Speaking Activity (p.254–255) and briefly discusses their meaning, inviting students to connect each to Karan's situation in the transcript they just heard.

Pairs prepare and perform a quick role-play for each of the three proverbs (p.254–255): Proverb 1 — judging by appearance then discovering true personality; Proverb 2 — talking about improvement versus actually putting in effort; Proverb 3 — giving up on a tough task versus persevering. Two or three pairs share for each proverb; class gives brief feedback on how naturally the proverb was used.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript theme — Karan doubting himself before a performance despite sustained practice — directly mirrors the poem's message, so a brief verbal bridge between the two strengthens comprehension. For the true/false listening task, students commonly mark statement 1 as true (the boy is actually nervous, not confident); slow down on that statement when reading the second time. For speaking, circulate during pair preparation to ensure students are framing genuine role-play situations rather than simply reciting the proverb.
materials: Transcript text (Unit 8, p.275 of transcript booklet)

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Speech and Exploring Inspiring Leaders

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.255–256): draft a speech on 'Turning Challenges into Opportunities' with formal guidelines
Learning Beyond the Text (p.256–257): research and present an inspiring leader's story in class

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the assembly speech context from Writing Task (p.255–256): the topic 'Turning Challenges into Opportunities', the three-part structure (opening, body, conclusion), and the expectation of formal register with a persuasive tone. Students annotate the guidelines in their textbooks.

Guided drafting: teacher models the opening paragraph live (greeting, a quotation or question, overview), then students draft their own opening and the two body paragraphs independently, using transition words and drawing on the poem's ideas or the Karan–Ananya conversation as anecdotal material. Teacher circulates offering brief formative prompts on structure and register.

Peer-response round: partners exchange drafts and check one item — does the speech close with a lasting statement and a clear thank-you? Students make a quick revision note before handing drafts back. Speeches are complete and self-contained at this point.

Launch of the Learning Beyond the Text project (p.256–257): teacher briefly introduces the three example leaders — Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, Lal Bahadur Shastri, Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam — and the expectation of finding a local personality. Two or three students share a first thought about whom they might research; teacher notes the range to avoid duplication. The research and presentation are independent work following this unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged with the poem's message of self-belief and the listening transcript's parallel on preparation and confidence, students have rich thematic material to draw on for the assembly speech. Watch for students who copy the poem's lines directly into the speech body — redirect them to paraphrase and attribute instead. The Beyond the Text research and class presentation are launched here as independent work; the project is self-directed from this point and does not require a further sitting to complete.

items.source_lo: Student analyses tone, central ideas, poetic devices (metaphor, antithesis, symbolism), and evaluates the poet's message using a motivational lyric as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Robert Langley's four-stanza lyric on self-belief, antithesis of aspiration and fear, and the hardest first step.
items.item_stem: Read the second stanza on p.246, beginning “Will it pull you forward”. Which statement best describes the central idea of this stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: Aspiration and fear pull in opposite directions, making choice difficult as the future nears.

options.label: B
options.text: Comfort and routine provide the best foundation for planning one’s future.

options.label: C
options.text: Confidence alone is enough to remove the difficulty of making life choices.

options.label: D
options.text: The future becomes easier to face once you have made a firm decision.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses resolution (stanza four) with the tension the second stanza establishes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misreads the poem’s critique of comfort, projecting a positive view of the status quo.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Anticipates the fourth stanza’s resolution rather than reading the second stanza on its own terms.

items.source_lo: Student analyses tone, central ideas, poetic devices (metaphor, antithesis, symbolism), and evaluates the poet's message using a motivational lyric as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Robert Langley's four-stanza lyric on self-belief, antithesis of aspiration and fear, and the hardest first step.
items.item_stem:
Read the third and fourth stanzas on p.246, beginning “There is such ease in comfort”. Answer the questions below.
1. How does Langley use the symbol of the ‘status quo’ in stanza three to argue against remaining in one’s comfort zone? What does it represent in the poem’s logic?
2. The poem’s final stanza closes with the line ‘You just need to believe in yourself / For your future to be on track.’ Evaluate whether this conclusion is satisfying or oversimplified, using evidence from the earlier stanzas to support your view.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the third and fourth stanzas on p.246, beginning “There is such ease in comfort”.

expected_elements: Q1: ‘Status quo’ symbolises stagnation, ease that prevents growth.
Q1: Student links comfort zone symbol to the poem’s warning against it.
Q2: Acknowledges the poem’s motivational force while noting it omits external obstacles.
Q2: Uses evidence from earlier stanzas (antithesis, fear, solitary challenge).
Q2: Articulates a reasoned evaluative position, not mere summary.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension by identifying key ideas and evaluating statements from an authentic spoken exchange using a dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Karan's pre-performance self-doubt and Ananya's reassurance that confidence grows through action despite nerves.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Karan and Ananya. Select ALL statements below that are TRUE according to what you hear.
(1) Karan worries he will forget his lines or freeze on stage.
(2) Ananya tells Karan that nervousness disappears entirely with enough rehearsal.
(3) Ananya says confidence comes from taking action even when one does not feel fully ready.
(4) Karan decides to withdraw from the play to avoid the pressure.
(5) Ananya believes that pushing through pressure is part of how a person grows.

options.text: Ananya believes that pushing through pressure is part of how a person grows.
Ananya says confidence comes from taking action even when one does not feel fully ready.
Ananya tells Karan that nervousness disappears entirely with enough rehearsal.
Karan decides to withdraw from the play to avoid the pressure.
Karan worries he will forget his lines or freeze on stage.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1, 3, and 5 are TRUE. Statement 2 is false — Ananya does not say nervousness disappears; she says pressure helps growth. Statement 4 is false — Karan resolves to give his best shot despite his nerves.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension by identifying key ideas and evaluating statements from an authentic spoken exchange using a dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Karan's pre-performance self-doubt and Ananya's reassurance that confidence grows through action despite nerves.
items.item_stem: Ananya tells Karan that ‘self-doubt is a normal part of big moments’. Based on what you heard in the conversation, explain in two or three sentences why Ananya considers Karan’s self-doubt normal, and what she says he should do despite feeling that way.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Ananya considers self-doubt normal because even a well-prepared performer like Karan — who has rehearsed for weeks — still feels it before a big moment. She says Karan should take action and give his best shot anyway, because confidence is built through doing, not through waiting until doubt disappears.

items.item_stem: With a partner, role-play the following situation: one of you has just joined a new class and is being judged unfairly by classmates who do not know you yet; the other is a friend who has taken time to understand you. In your conversation, use the proverb ‘Don’t judge a book by its cover’ naturally — do not simply state it, but show its truth through what you say and do. Aim for a clear two-sided exchange.

expected_elements: Proverb is embedded naturally in the dialogue, not announced.
Both roles are distinct and each student speaks substantively.
The scene shows unfair judgement giving way to genuine understanding.
Language is appropriate to a peer conversation; register is consistent.
Exchange has a clear turning point where first impression is revised.

items.item_stem: Your class is debating whether schools should require students to participate in a difficult public-speaking event even when they are afraid. Argue ONE side — either in favour or against — using the proverb ‘When the going gets tough, the tough get going’ as part of your argument. You must give at least two reasons for your position and respond to one point the other side might raise.

expected_elements: Clear position stated at the outset; proverb woven in as evidence.
At least two distinct reasons given for the chosen side.
An opposing viewpoint acknowledged and countered with rationale.
Formal enough register for a class debate; no informal hedging.
Argument is coherent and moves toward a reasoned conclusion.

items.item_stem: Your school is inviting students to speak at an inter-school event on the theme ‘Actions Speak Louder than Words’. Write a notice for your school notice board inviting students from Grades VIII to X to sign up to deliver a two-minute speech at the event. Your notice must include: the event name and date, what participants are expected to do, how and by when to register, and a brief sentence encouraging participation.

expected_elements: Correct notice format: heading, date/venue, body, sign-off.
All four required details present (event, task, registration, encouragement).
Formal, concise register appropriate to a school notice board.
Encouraging sentence motivates without becoming informal or casual.
No grammatical errors that impede clarity of the notice.

items.item_stem: A local newspaper has published an editorial arguing that school students spend too much time on self-improvement activities — speeches, clubs, performances — and too little time on academic study. Write a letter to the editor arguing against this view. In your letter: open with a clear position, give two reasoned arguments supported by real-life or textual evidence, address one counter-argument the editorial might raise, and close with a persuasive final appeal.

expected_elements: Correct letter-to-editor format: address, date, salutation, sign-off.
Clear opening stance stated in the first paragraph.
Two distinct arguments supported by reasoning or evidence.
Counter-argument acknowledged and effectively refuted.
Persuasive closing appeal; formal register maintained throughout.

items.item_stem: Match each Latin expression in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
et cetera | for example, such as
exempli gratia | and so on, and the rest
ad hoc | something given in return for something
quid pro quo | formed or done for a specific purpose
per se | in the middle of the action
in media res | by or in itself, intrinsically

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: et cetera — and so on, and the rest; exempli gratia — for example, such as; ad hoc — formed or done for a specific purpose; quid pro quo — something given in return for something; per se — by or in itself, intrinsically; in media res — in the middle of the action.

answer_key.right: and so on, and the rest
formed or done for a specific purpose
something given in return for something
in the middle of the action

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies Latin expressions borrowed into English and analyses the function and effect of rhetorical questions in persuasive contexts using vocabulary-in-context as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Latin expressions active in English prose and rhetorical questions drawn from the poem's persuasive register.
items.item_stem:
The poem asks, ‘Will it pull you forward / Or push you back in fear?’ — a rhetorical question that does not expect a direct answer. Read the two statements below and, for each, write one sentence explaining the specific persuasive effect the rhetorical question achieves.
(i) ‘If not now, when will we ever stand up for what is right?’
(ii) ‘Is staying comfortable really the same as moving forward?’

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) This rhetorical question creates urgency and a sense of moral obligation, implying that the time for action is the present moment. (ii) This rhetorical question challenges the reader to reconsider the value of comfort, strongly implying that staying comfortable is not the same as making progress — mirroring the poem’s critique of the status quo.

items.item_stem: Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam delivered newspapers as a child to support his family’s income before rising to become the 11th President of India and one of the country’s leading scientists. Write a paragraph of eight to ten sentences describing how Kalam’s life journey illustrates the poem’s message that ‘the first step is the hardest’ and that self-belief is essential for growth. Use at least one specific fact about his life and connect it explicitly to the poem.

expected_elements: At least one specific biographical fact about Kalam included accurately.
Explicit link drawn between Kalam’s hardship and the poem’s message.
The phrase or idea of self-belief connected to a specific life choice he made.
Paragraph is coherent and organised, not a list of disconnected facts.
Student’s own interpretive voice present, not only summary.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents the story of a real person who turned adversity into achievement, connecting personal biography to the poem's theme of self-belief using interdisciplinary project-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Indian leaders — Ambedkar, Shastri, Kalam — and a locally sourced personality who overcame hardship.
items.item_stem: Identify a person from your own village, town, city, or state who overcame significant difficulty to achieve something meaningful — this may be someone in education, the arts, sports, public service, or any other field. Prepare a project presentation that includes: (a) a brief biography of the person with at least two specific facts; (b) the nature of the challenge they faced and how they responded; (c) a direct comparison with one leader from the examples given in the unit (Ambedkar, Shastri, or Kalam); and (d) a closing reflection on what their story adds to your understanding of the poem’s message about self-belief.

expected_elements: Local personality chosen is real and identifiable; two facts given.
Nature of adversity and the person’s response described specifically.
Comparison with Ambedkar, Shastri, or Kalam is substantive, not superficial.
Closing reflection connects the biography to the poem’s theme of self-belief.
Presentation is organised and student’s own analytical voice is evident.
